text: The Rastriya Swatantra Party (Nepali: राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी, lit. 'National Independence Party', abbr. RSP) is a centrist political party in Nepal.[2][3][5] It was announced by Rabi Lamichhane in June 2022[10] and registered with the Election Commission of Nepal on 1 July 2022, ahead of the 2022 Nepalese general election.[11][12] The party was formally registered on that date with Rabi Lamichhane as the founding president and a bell inside a circle as its election symbol.[15] On 16 June 2022, Lamichhane resigned as managing director of Galaxy 4K television and announced his candidacy for the House of Representatives in the 2022 general elections.[13] On 21 June 2022, he announced the formation of the RSP along with a 21-member central committee.[10][14] The party fielded 131 candidates in First Past the Post constituencies and submitted a closed list of 107 prospective members for proportional representation seats in the House of Representatives, without fielding any candidates for provincial assemblies. Candidates were selected through primary elections.[16] The RSP emerged as the fourth-largest national party in Nepal after the 2022 election, securing victory in seven constituencies—four in Kathmandu, one in Lalitpur, and two in Chitwan—and receiving 10.70% of the party list vote, becoming one of the seven national parties in the Federal Parliament. It won 13 seats via proportional representation, bringing its total parliamentary strength to 20.[18][19] The party later won the Tanahun 1 constituency, where Swarnim Wagle was elected and advocated for reducing the number of army personnel. The party was a junior ally in the Prachanda-led government from 26 December 2022 to 5 February 2023 and served as a coalition partner with four cabinet ministries from 6 March 2024 to 12 July 2024.[6][7][8][9] Party president Rabi Lamichhane fled from Nakkhu jail during the 2025 Nepalese Gen Z protests, claiming it was per the decision of the Ministry of Home Affairs, a claim rejected by the prison administration and criticized as indirectly enabling imprisoned individuals to escape.[21][22][23] Party leaders were divided over dissolving parliament, with Sobita Gautam condemning such a move.[24] Joint general secretary and former MP Sumana Shrestha resigned from her post and from party membership on 14 September 2025 amid protests, citing a culture of leader worship.[25][26] Party chief whip Santosh Pariyar left the party to form the Pragatisheel Loktantrik Party, stating that personality-based leadership cannot lead to national development.[27][28] The party announced it would have no sister organizations, only members, not cadres, and emphasized primary elections for candidate selection.[14][10] The RSP supports constitutional socialism, market socialism, progressivism, political pragmatism, participatory democracy, economic liberalism,[2] and political freedom.[29] It endorses a "capitalistic" economy with individual rights, asserting that industrial and commercial activities are off-limits to government interference, as economic freedom drives prosperity and government planning disrupts the economy.[33][34][35][36] The party supports recall elections, the right to reject, and absentee ballots, and advocates for a directly elected prime minister and directly elected chief ministers for the seven provinces.[10][14][37] In its 2022 election manifesto, it proposed a non-partisan president elected by an expanded electoral college including ward chairs and federal lawmakers, and suggested the chairman of the National Assembly act as de facto vice-president. It also called for ending political appointments in constitutional bodies, scrapping the Constitutional Council, and having appointments recommended by the National Assembly and confirmed by the House of Representatives. The party advocated dissolving provincial assemblies and district coordination committees, favoring instead a provincial council elected by local government heads. Rabi Lamichhane did not cast a vote in the 2022 provincial elections.[39][40] The party views the private sector, cooperatives, and public sector as the three pillars of the economy, favors competition, and seeks to expand the private sector's role as an alternative to the public sector for service delivery and economic growth. It supports ending income tax for individuals in the lowest octile of earners, establishing food banks in every ward, and providing nutrition assistance to those below the poverty line through ration cards. It also seeks to expand the social welfare system and include private insurance companies. The party supports a single-payer healthcare system, with at least one laboratory and a 750-bed hospital in each province, a 50 to 100-bed hospital in each of the 77 districts, a 6 to 25-bed hospital in each local unit, and a clinic in every ward. It wants a centralized national ambulance service, a health and quality assurance accreditation board, a food and drug department, a central disease board, and a health innovation & development board, along with a health workers act for public healthcare workers.[41] To combat corruption, it supports a Whistleblower Protection Act and an Anti-Corruption Police under the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority.[41] The party also calls for shelters for abuse victims and a fund for victims of human trafficking, domestic violence, and acid attacks, and promotes entrepreneurship among women and sexual minorities by establishing funds where at least sixty percent of shareholders or employees are female or from a sexual minority group.[41] The party nominated 131 candidates for the First Past the Post seats in the 2022 general election.[42] This list of MPs is based on the order of power holdings within the party, ministry level, and length of presence in House of Representatives meetings.
